newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - World's second biggest library braves cash squeeze.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - World's second biggest library braves cash squeeze.

text.p: With its imposing concrete facade and bold friezes depicting heroic workers and peasants, the Russian State Library seems to embody the pride that helped turn the Soviet Union into an intellectual superpower.

But like most post-Soviet cultural institutions the library, said to be the world's second biggest after Washington's Library of Congress, is struggling to pay its bills and survive the country's painful transition to a market-oriented economy.
"We cannot escape the general economic malaise affecting the country. We are up to our necks in debt. Things are very tough," said the library's director Vladimir Yegorov.

Known in communist times as the Lenin Library after the Soviet state founder and still affectionately called the Leninka by Muscovites, the library sits grandly in the heart of the capital, a short stroll from the Kremlin walls.

With its soaring columns, maze of reading rooms and marble staircases it is built on a monumental scale, as befits its status as the nation's pre-eminent library owning some 42 million books, manuscripts and other documents in 247 languages.
"It's not so much a library as a town," said Svetlana who works there.
"It would take a week to show you everything," she said, walking through the biggest reading room with its ornate green desk lamps under the proud gaze of a Lenin statue.
LIBRARY HAS PROUD PAST BUT OVERSHADOWED BY POLITICS

Founded in 1862, the library was frequented in the past by some of Russia's greatest writers such as Leo Tolstoy, Fyodor Dostoevsky and Anton Chekhov, and by scientists like Dmitry Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table.

After the 1917 revolution that turned Russia into the world's first communist state, Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin found time to work at the library despite a hectic work schedule and took a personal interest in building up its collection.
The library has manuscripts dating back to the sixth century and reputedly contains a copy of every book ever published in the Soviet Union and post-communist Russia.

In Soviet times this meant the library had to carefully control readers' access to books to ensure they did not fall under the influence of authors like dissident novelist Alexander Solzhenitsyn deemed ideologically unacceptable.
At the height of dictator Josef Stalin's purges books by disgraced scientists and officials were quietly and regularly moved from open shelves to the classified "Spetzkhran" section.
Some only survive in the Leninka because all other copies were destroyed.
CASH WOES HAMPER MODERNISATION
The library also boasts large collections of European, Oriental and Middle Eastern books and manuscripts and has a unique collection that once belonged to Russia's imperial dynasty, the Romanovs.

"We are not only a library. We are a centre of research and we restore and preserve documents and manuscripts," Yegorov told Reuters in an interview in his elegant, panelled study decorated with busts of classical philosophers.
But he said the library's financial woes were hampering its efforts to take advantage of today's advances in information technology.
"We have recently been connected to the Internet but the lack of money means we cannot develop as a genuine, pioneering centre of study and research," said Yegorov.
He said the library managed to pay its employees' salaries in full and on time -- no mean feat in Russia's cash-starved public sector where millions often go many months without pay.
But it has no money left over even for basic maintenance.
"Leaving aside the money we get to pay staff wages, so far this year we have received only about three percent of the funds allocated to us by the state budget," he said.
The library's annual budget, excluding wages, should total 120 billion roubles ($20.8 million) but in 1996 it received only 22 percent of the money due to it.

Asked about the liberal-minded government's current drive to cut state spending, Yegorov said the plan, known as sequestration, was meant to reduce the budget across the board to 55 percent of initial levels.
"If spending cuts mean we get 55 percent of our budget I would be very happy," he added with an ironic smile.
"Fortunately both the federal and municipal government understand our predicament. They have not yet turned off the water or the electricity," he said.
LIBRARY TRYING TO TAP OUTSIDE FUNDS

The cash squeeze means that the library is unable to offer its quarter of a million members adequate services and Yegorov worries about the implications of savings on security, fire prevention, lifts and storage facilities.
"We also have problems with lack of space. The reading rooms are very cramped," he said.
A few years ago disturbing reports circulated that the library's very foundations were threatened by erosion caused by the construction of the Borovitskaya metro station directly underneath it.
"We were alarmed about the possible repercussions but exhaustive studies showed that in fact there was no serious subsidence and that the site was stable," he said.

Much of the library's collection is housed in storage rooms outside Moscow where, despite the lack of money, the necessary conditions of temperature, humidity and security still meet international standards, Yegorov said.
Helped by the Moscow city authorities, the library is trying to attract outside funds and a French firm is participating in a programme to computerise and update its cataloguing systems.
Around 5,000 people use the library daily. Anybody with a passport, including foreigners, can easily join, though Yegorov regrets that a small token membership fee may soon have to be charged.

"We are determined that students, who make up about 40 percent of our users, should pay less, for example, than bankers, reflecting the ability to pay," said Yegorov, still imbued with the paternalistic ethic of Soviet times.
"But without financial stabilisation there can be no long-term resolution of our problems."
($ = 5775 Russian Roubles)
